title: Jesus's prayer at the supper (CCC 2746–2751)
hook: John 17, the prayer of the hour
tomorrow: The whole gospel in a prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the battle of prayer: distraction, dryness, weariness, and the widow who wouldn't quit. Your line was keep coming back. How many small returns did you count? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

The supper is over. The feet have been washed. Judas has gone out into the night. For chapters, John's Gospel has let Jesus talk to his friends at the table: about a vine and its branches, about a helper who will come, about a sorrow that will turn to joy. And then, with the garden and the arrest only a short walk away, he stops talking to them. He lifts his eyes and starts talking to his Father, out loud, with them still in the room. They get to overhear it. So do we. Today: Jesus's prayer at the supper.
screen: `THE SUPPER IS OVER.` → `HE STOPS TALKING TO THEM.` → `THEY OVERHEAR HIM PRAY.`

segments.voice: It opens in John 17, in the Douay-Rheims: "Father, the hour is come, glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee." The hour. Earlier in John's Gospel, his hour had not yet come. Now it has. The Catechism calls this the prayer of the hour of Jesus, and says Christian tradition rightly names it his priestly prayer: a high priest praying, on the edge of offering himself. Then it moves outward, in rings. First he prays for himself, to finish the work he was given. Then for the friends in the room. And here's the line that surprises: "I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil." He doesn't ask for their escape. He asks for them to be kept, right where they are. Then the ring widens again, past the room, past that night. "And not for them only do I pray, but for them also who through their word shall believe in me." Catholics hear that line as including every believer who came after, down to today. And what he asks for them is "That they all may be one." The Catechism adds that this prayer doesn't stop when the night ends. Like his sacrifice, it says, it reaches to the end of time. And it notices something else: the requests of the Our Father are already here, folded in. The Father's name. His work finished. His people kept from evil. In the Catholic reading, the prayer he taught and the prayer he prayed are one.
screen: `FATHER, THE HOUR IS COME.` · `KEEP THEM FROM EVIL.` · `FOR THOSE WHO WILL BELIEVE.` · `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read John 17. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, open to John chapter seventeen and read it slowly, as far as you get in the time. If you can't, hold one line from today: "That they all may be one." Settle, and breathe. Notice who's in each ring: himself, his friends, people not yet born. If you pray, you can let yourself be one of the ones he prays for. If you don't, just stay with what he asks. The bell holds the time.
Jesus's prayer at the supper. John 17, which the Catechism calls the prayer of the hour, his priestly prayer for his friends and for all who would believe through them. Today's words.
screen: `JESUS'S PRAYER AT THE SUPPER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: his prayer for us. Today, notice one person you don't agree with who shares your faith, or your family, or your street, and remember the words that they all may be one. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

original.note: Greek: the hour — "Father, the hour is come," the opening of John 17.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long goodbye speech at the end of John's Gospel.
what it means: Jesus prays aloud to the Father, for himself, his friends, and all who would believe through them, that they all may be one.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism calls it the prayer of the hour and, with tradition, his priestly prayer, and finds the Our Father's petitions folded inside it.

notes: CCC 2746–2751 paraphrased (copyrighted English). Check: 'the prayer of the hour of Jesus' and tradition rightly calling it the 'priestly' prayer (2747), the prayer extending to the end of time like his sacrifice (2749), the Our Father's petitions present in John 17 (2750).
'Earlier in John's Gospel, his hour had not yet come' rests on John 2:4, 7:30, 8:20 (with 12:23, 13:1); confirm phrasing.
The rings structure (himself, the disciples, later believers) is a common reading of John 17:1–5, 6–19, 20–26; confirm it is fair as stated.
